lesson.subtitle: Lesson 20 -- Milestone Review: Twenty Days
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Patrícia Yamaguti | Lesson 20 -- Milestone Review

listenings.text: People always ask me about the big moments abroad: the airport, the police, the hospital. But the truth is that the big moments are rare, and the ordinary day is what really changes. Let me tell you about one Tuesday. In the morning I read the sign at the museum and I saw it was closed, so we did not cross the city for nothing. At eleven I called and booked for Wednesday instead, and I understood the last entry time. At lunch I ordered for four people and I asked about the nuts, because my son is allergic. In the afternoon I bought a coat for my daughter, in another colour, because the first one was not in her size and I asked. At the till I did not understand the total, so I asked the man to write it down, and he did, and nobody looked at me. And in the evening I sat on a bench for twenty minutes with another mother, and we talked about nothing at all. Not one emergency. That was the day everything changed.

After twenty lessons, students always ask me the same question: am I better, or am I the same? And it is a fair question, because progress at this level is invisible from the inside. So I tell them to stop measuring the wrong thing. Do not count the words you know. Count the situations you no longer avoid. At the start, most of my students avoid the shop, the telephone and the conversation with no purpose. Those three are the real map. If today you go into a shop alone, if you can call somebody and book a table, and if you can sit next to a stranger for ten minutes without looking at your phone, then you are not the same person who started, even if your grammar is exactly as it was. And one more thing, and please believe me on this: the ones who ask people to repeat learn faster than the ones who pretend to understand. Always.

reading.rtitle: One Ordinary Tuesday -- a page from a travel diary
paras: People ask me about the big moments abroad: the airport, the hospital, the police. But the big moments are rare. It is the ordinary day that shows you what changed, and this was an ordinary Tuesday.

In the morning I read the sign on the door of the museum, and it said closed on Mondays and Tuesdays. Before, I would have crossed the city with two children and found the door shut. Instead I called, I asked what time they open, I understood that the last entry is half past four, and I booked for Wednesday morning, four people.

At lunch I ordered for the four of us. I asked whether the pasta had nuts in it, because my son is allergic, and the waiter checked. In the afternoon I bought a coat for my daughter. It was not in her size on the shelf, so I asked if they had it in the back, and then in another colour, and the second answer was yes.

At the till I did not understand the total. I asked the man to say it again, and then I asked him to write it down, and he did, and nobody in the queue looked at me. In the evening I sat on a bench for twenty minutes with another mother and we talked about our children and about nothing at all. Not one emergency in the whole day. That is the day I know I am not the same.
